text: The claims agree that rationale is valuable but rarely captured: developers may lack motivation to document it without immediate benefit, and mining latent rationale from issue logs, when fed to LLMs, was reported to yield 10×-18× more full-match patches in program repair.

Agent-side provenance is reported as weak: coding agents leave decision trails that are hard to reconstruct, and current practice lacks version-control-like provenance tracking, though the supporting report rests on practitioner observation and project artifacts, not a controlled study.

Failure history is partly recoverable from trajectories: failed ones are longer, more variable and differ by agent, and most trajectories find the right files even when failing. Yet the length–failure link is reported to reverse once task difficulty is controlled, so surface trace features are unreliable indicators.

Automated failure attribution is reported as limited: an LLM judge reached only 0.14-0.52 step-level accuracy on one benchmark, counterfactual replay is reliable but its cost grows linearly, and one categorization of unresolved trajectories was validated on only 15 hand-labelled instances.

Intent is the central difficulty. Inferring developer intent or specification is called the toughest repair challenge, and one analysis attributed 51.7% of 207 unresolved tasks to ambiguous issue descriptions.

Traceability results pull apart: individual LLM studies report strong figures such as 100% precision and 78.5% recall in one setting, while a survey chapter says no automated approach suffices for safety-critical systems and that scaling is unclear.
Passing tests is reported as insufficient evidence of correctness, so test intent recovered from agent traces cannot be assumed to certify patches.

The claims support that design rationale mined from issue discussion can be reused to help repair, and that past fix patterns are a reusable source of guidance. This is not shown for rationale recovered from agent traces themselves.
Failure information in trajectories carries signal, but attributing failures reliably is reported to be limited and costly.
Requirements traceability recovery shows promising but uneven results, with unresolved concerns about datasets, scale and safety-critical use.

Test intent is not shown to be reliably recoverable or sufficient, since passing tests may still hide overfitting. Whether any category improves maintainability from agent traces specifically remains unanswered by these claims.
Run controlled studies, beyond practitioner observation, of whether provenance and decision trails captured from agent runs can be reconstructed and reused for maintenance.
Validate trajectory failure categorization against larger hand-labelled sets, controlling for task difficulty.
Develop cheaper failure attribution that improves on the low judge accuracy without the linear cost of replay.

Test whether design-rationale mining, which DRMiner performs on Jira issue logs, transfers to agent traces. DRMiner reports that rationale-prompted LLMs generate 10×-18× more full-match patches, and that developers lack motivation to document rationales, so rationales have no standard capture. The evidence comes from issue logs, not agent traces.
Measure traceability recovery on real safety-critical data with larger credible datasets, and examine scaling.

Evaluate whether recovered test intent and specifications, such as the reproducer tests, patch explanations and accumulated specifications that SpecRover's reviewer produces as evidence of correctness, can detect overfitting patches beyond passing tests. AutoCodeRover's authors acknowledge that a patch passing the added tests may still overfit, and the test-driven survey concludes that passing tests alone does not establish behavioral equivalence.
